A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Pro-Pose and contain readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, references, and supplementary material. Retained content can be matched across the substantial formatting and numbering changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original DeepFashion and WPose evaluations, training-data and personalization ablations, and supplementary identity-overfitting analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds Gemini comparisons, standardized-input controls, pose-stratified identity analysis, and qualitative application demonstrations.

M1.justification: v1 explicitly restricts UV conditioning to the face and personalization loss to a facial mask. v2 extends conditioning to full-body UV textures, illustrated in Figure 3, and changes the personalization mask to visible skin/foreground in Section 3.5. This materially expands the conditioning and optimization scope, while retaining the Flux backbone, donor-mask mechanism, and paired/unpaired training framework.

E1.justification: The existing training sources and evaluation datasets are retained. v2 adds distinct application tasks: downstream garment transfer through Google Virtual Try-On and controlled texture editing through a manually added tattoo (Sections 4.4–4.5). These are demonstrated qualitatively rather than through new quantitative benchmarks.

E2.justification: Gemini 2.5 Flash Image changes from a preprocessing tool into an evaluated comparator in Table 1, the facial-region table, and qualitative comparisons. The five existing pose-generation baselines remain. The new downstream comparison also evaluates Google VTO directly versus Google VTO using Pro-Pose preprocessing.

E3.justification: v2 introduces BC-preprocessed baseline-input controls, head-pose-change stratification using Euler-angle differences, and a FaceSim < 0.4 failure criterion. It also adds direct-versus-preprocessed VTO testing. Existing test-pair counts and training budgets remain unchanged. Appendix A revises Prompt V1 to specify 3-inch shorts; this documents a preprocessing revision without establishing dataset regeneration.

E4.justification: New analyses test identity robustness across pose difficulty (Figure 6) and whether clothing preprocessing explains the comparison advantage (Appendix D.3). v2 also adds texture-editing and VTO case studies and replaces the tattoo-loss failure example with a body-estimation failure. The earlier donor-mask, training-data, personalization, and identity-overfitting analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 6 newly displays shaded ranges around pose-binned FaceSim curves. Their statistical meaning and construction are unspecified, so they cannot reliably be identified as confidence intervals or standard deviations. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts or seeds; the earlier identity-distribution plots are retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises Pro-Pose and training-variant scores: full-model DeepFashion FaceSim changes from 0.5919 to 0.6047, and WPose M-PSNR from 19.87 to 19.95. These accompany the method revision and do not isolate its effect. v2 adds Gemini results, BC-input results, pose-stratified findings, and application examples. Tables 2–3 remain numerically unchanged, as do existing facial-region entries relocated from Table 4 to Table 5.

T1.justification: Equation 9 retains its algebraic form but redefines its mask from the facial region to skin/visible foreground, changing the objective's mathematical support. The donor-mask reasoning, flow formulation, and supplementary UV-extraction derivation otherwise remain equivalent; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim that Pro-Pose provides a canonical intermediate that improves downstream VTO. They also assert full-body UV-based identity preservation, including visible skin details, whereas v1 leaves body-texture conditioning as future work. The original donor-reposing and hybrid-training contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the face-only-conditioning limitation with specific explanations of SMPL-X shape-estimation errors and unrecoverable self-occluded body regions. It newly attributes VTO improvements to removing source-clothing interference and interprets the BC-input control as evidence for methodological gains. Extreme-pose hallucination and the earlier identity-overfitting interpretation remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the Gemini comparison prompt in Figure 12, explicitly labels main results as zero-shot, and discloses combining source-estimated body shape with target pose during evaluation. It also revises the garment-editing prompt. Backbone, optimizer, hardware, dropout, donor-pool, and few-shot training details are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Google Try-On tool reference and positions Pro-Pose as a preprocessing complement to existing VTO systems. The previous 57 references and the related-work taxonomy are retained, apart from ordering and bibliographic formatting changes.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites emphasize full-body identity and downstream VTO, refine terminology, and clarify zero-shot evaluation. Most methodological and supplementary prose retains its sequence and substance. References move before the supplement, whose numbered sections become Appendices A–E.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a narrower single-column format with extensive resizing and repositioning. Figure 1 is redesigned around VTO; new displays cover pose difficulty, texture editing, VTO, and BC-input comparisons. Existing comparison grids gain Gemini panels and additional examples, Figure 3 shows body textures, and the limitations figure is revised.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation credibility: the new BC-input control addresses an important preprocessing confound in v1, and Gemini supplies a stronger additional comparison. The explicit body-estimation limitation also improves interpretation. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: Figure 4 still describes a facial loss, Figure 6 leaves its bands undefined and overgeneralizes the failure-rate comparison, and downstream VTO claims rely on limited qualitative examples.
